title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Pulse-check decisions
Learners will practice:

Preparing a pulse check before the pause
Making a shock/no-shock call under uncertainty
Preventing airway/procedure pauses
Using EtCO2 and other signals when ROSC is uncertain

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Code blue on E50
Compressions are ongoing when you arrive.
You establish yourself as code leader.
Prompt: You have 20 seconds before the next pulse check. What do you assign?

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Before the pause
Try:

“Recorder, call out pause time.”


“You check pulse.”


“You call rhythm.”


“Defib team, be ready if shockable.”


“Everyone else: compressions resume unless I say shock.”

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
First pulse check
No palpable pulse

Shock, no shock, or uncertain?Prompt: Shock, no shock, or uncertain?

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Fine VF vs asystole
If uncertain:

Turn up gain.
Check leads/connection.
Voice your uncertainty.
If it could be VF/pVT, shock (consider consequences of each error).
If not, resume CPR.


Coarse vs fine ventricular fibrillation

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Second pulse check
No palpable pulse

Airway team ready to intubate, asks for a moment before resuming compressionsAnswer:

“Airway, keep working during compressions. We’ll give you the next planned pause only if you are ready.”


“If intubation will interrupt CPR, put in an LMA.”

Airway does not own the pause.

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
What really matters
During arrest, protect two things:

Compression fraction
Early defibrillation for shockable rhythm

Everything else has to fit around those.

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Make uncertainty public and brief
Name what is uncertain, then name the action.
Try:

“I am uncertain whether this is fine VF or asystole. Gain up and check leads now.”


“If this could be VF/pVT after the quick check, we shock. If not, compressions resume.”


“Possible ROSC. At the next check: rhythm, pulse, waveform.”


“If not convincing, resume compressions.”

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Confirming ROSC can be hard
Consider the consequences of each error.


Use:

EtCO2 trend or sudden rise
Arterial line or pleth waveform if present
Doppler if ready
POCUS only if pre-positioned
Clinical signs





Use EtCO2 to help detect ROSC



When in doubt, continue compressions.
No probe fishing during pulse checks.

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Third pulse check

EtCO2 = 36 mmHgPrompt: What do you say?
Suggested answer:

“Possible ROSC. At the next check: rhythm, pulse, waveform. If not convincing, resume compressions.”

title: Pulse-Check Decisions: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Summary
Do not miss fine VF.
Do not prolong pauses for procedures.
Do not keep uncertainty private.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Leadership in the first 60 seconds
Learners will practice:

Naming who is leading
Anchoring the room
Making the working problem and plan public
Inviting concern before action

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Case start
Rapid response to S408
Sign-out: “81M, SVT, now stable.”
Now: HR 160, MAP 85 -> 70, lightheaded.
A bedside nurse says: “He looks worse than he did 10 minutes ago.”
Prompt: Before choosing a medication, what do you say to the room?

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Say the sentence
Try:

“I’m [name], the senior medicine resident responding to the rapid. Who is currently coordinating this response?”

Then choose:

“Okay, I’ll run the room.”


“Can I take over?”


“Okay, I’ll support. Who is making final decisions?”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Failure mode
Ways this commonly goes wrong:

Multiple teams entered.
No one named who owned the response.
The resident’s plan and the primary/CV plan diverged.
A medication order lacked clear dose, owner, and readback.
The nurse’s clarification was the safety signal.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Anchor the room
If you are leading:

Stay visible.
Do not become the task person.
Assign roles by name, badge, or function.
Keep the patient, monitor, bedside nurse, doorway, and task flow in view.

Try:

“I’m going to stay here and run the room. Please bring questions or data to me.”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Make the plan public
Try:

“I think [problem] is the issue. I’m worried about [risk]. My plan is [plan].”

Then ask:

“What are we missing?”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Invite expertise without losing leadership
Try:

“Bedside nurse, what changed?”


“Outreach nurse, what are you most worried about?”


“Pharmacy, help me confirm dose and contraindications.”

Leadership is not proving you can do the tasks yourself.
Stay findable, keep the plan public, and delegate task work by name.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Summary
Four moves

Name the leadership state.
Anchor yourself.
Say the working problem and first plan.
Invite concern before action.

Next: apply the same leadership clarity to pulse-check decisions. The nurse-response module later builds on this language for bedside and outreach collaboration.

Case 4
36F admitted for ETOH detox.
RRT activated on third day of admission.
Tachycardic, HR 180s, dizzy/lightheaded but responsive, pulsatile in all ext.

Team interface prompt
The outreach nurse arrived before you and has already tried vagal maneuvers.
Start with:

“Can I get the 30-second story: what changed, what have you tried, and what are you worried about?”

Then state whether this is stable, unstable, or peri-arrest.

title: Case 4
text:
Teaching Points

Adenosine is for stable, regular, monomorphic tachycardia when SVT or regular monomorphic WCT is possible. Do not give it for unstable, irregular, or polymorphic WCT.
If the rhythm is narrow and fast, decide whether it is causing instability or reflecting another problem.

title: Case 2
section: After ROSC: stabilize before you celebrate
text:
After ROSC: stabilize before you celebrate

12-lead ECG as soon as feasible.
Oxygen: 100% until reliable SpO2/PaO2, then SpO2 90-98%.
Ventilation: PaCO2 35-45 if comatose and ventilated.
Pressure: avoid hypotension; minimum MAP >=65.
If unresponsive: protocolized temperature control >=36 hours.
Ask: coronary, PE, tamponade, hemorrhage, pneumothorax, toxic/metabolic?

title: Case 2
text:
Team interface prompt
The nurse who called the code saw the telemetry alarm and knows when the patient lost pulses.
Ask:

“What rhythm triggered the alarm, when did compressions start, and has the first shock happened?”

Close the loop on shock timing and post-ROSC ECG.

title: Case 2
text:
Teaching Points

Time to first shock is critical in VF
Role of antiarrhythmics is adjunctive, not primary
Persisting VF/pVT: follow device energy strategy; if unsure, maximum biphasic energy is reasonable. Protect compression fraction and confirm pads/contact. Do not teach routine DSED/vector-change as standard care.
VF/VT: Think.. acute MI (sudden, chest pain), electrolyte derangements, drug toxicity

title: Facilitators
text:
Nurse-Team Co-Facilitation
For the 2026 iteration, invite at least one nurse rapid response, code team, or critical care outreach lead to review the collaboration module before teaching.
If feasible, include a nurse co-facilitator for one scenario station. Their role is to help learners practice how to ask for bedside context, clarify leadership, and close the loop without undermining nursing expertise.
Use this nurse-response debrief checklist after the station:

Did the resident identify who was coordinating?
Did the resident ask the bedside nurse for trajectory?
Did the resident ask outreach what had already been tried?
Did the resident make the working problem and immediate plan public?
Did the resident respond constructively to nursing concern?
Did the resident close the loop on orders, disposition, ownership, and escalation trigger?

text:
The scenarios are designed for in-person practice with the Zoll. Use the public slides for learner review; facilitator-specific prompts belong in the instructor guide.
Each case now includes a brief resident/nurse-team interface prompt: who has bedside context, what the resident should ask, and how the plan should be closed-looped.


Case 1
Pulseless patient with severe metabolic derangements. Focus: asystole versus fine VF, the less-bad error when uncertain, and using nurse recorder/timekeeper input during rhythm checks.
Open case


Case 2
Pulseless VF/VT physiology with post-ROSC decision-making. Focus: first shock, persisting VF/pVT guardrails, post-ROSC stabilization, and cause search.
Open case


Case 3
Polymorphic VT/TdP after QT-prolonging medications. Focus: immediate unsynchronized high-energy shock for sustained polymorphic VT, long-QT/TdP recognition, and pharmacy/nursing medication-history input.
Open case


Case 4
Tachycardia during an RRT. Focus: rhythm interpretation, stability assessment, adenosine guardrails, escalation, and the first 30-second huddle.
Open case


Case 5
Bradycardia with hypotension and confusion. Focus: complete heart block, atropine limits, pacing pads, transcutaneous pacing setup, sedation planning, and shared preparation with bedside nursing.

title: 2026 Code Blue and Rapid Response Seminar
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the session, learners should be able to:

Make the leadership state clear on arrival: lead, support, consult, or transition leadership explicitly.
Prepare pulse checks, make shock/no-shock decisions public, and protect compression pauses.
Use bedside nurse and outreach trajectory to align roles, plan, orders, ownership, and escalation triggers.
Decide when the current room is unsafe and activate the appropriate site-specific resource or destination.
Close each rapid/code with explicit disposition, order owner, handoff point, family plan when needed, and debrief.







Tip



Didactics alone have limits. Regular review, simulation, interprofessional practice, and feedback after real events are what turn these skills into reflexes.

title: 2026 Code Blue and Rapid Response Seminar
text:
Why This Course Exists
Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership is not just algorithm recall. The resident leader has to make the room work: make the leadership state explicit, make roles visible, keep communication psychologically safe, integrate bedside expertise, and escalate resources before the response stalls.
Stakeholders from Code Blue and Rapid Response teams, including senior residents, nurses, respiratory therapists, and quality leads, identified four recurring hazards during resident-led responses:

Unclear team leadership, which can cause role confusion, low psychological safety, and decreased collaboration. (Steinbach et al. 2024)
Failure to cardiovert or defibrillate shockable rhythms.
Delayed critical decisions, including calling for help, initial stabilization, and transport to ICU.
Poorly defined collaboration between residents and bedside nurses, nurse-led rapid response teams, or critical care outreach teams.

This seminar targets those hazards through brief micro-skills, discussion, hands-on scenarios, and interprofessional scripts that can be used during real events.

title: Resources
text: Quick reference materials for Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership.

title: Resources
text:
Key Points

Name the leadership state early. Ask who is coordinating, then lead, support, consult, or transition leadership explicitly.
Get the nursing trajectory. Ask bedside and outreach nurses what changed, what has been tried, and what worries them most.
Protect pulse checks. Prepare the pause, make shock/no-shock and pulse/no-pulse decisions public, and resume compressions quickly when uncertain.
Ask whether the patient is safe here. Identify the missing resource, destination, owner, and escalation trigger.
Close the loop before leaving. Name disposition, orders, ownership, and the trigger for calling RRT, ICU, or code response.

title: Resources
text:
Nurse-Team Huddle Script


“Let’s huddle for 30 seconds. I’m [name], responding as the senior medicine resident. Who is coordinating? Bedside nurse, what changed? Outreach, what have you tried and what worries you most? Primary team, baseline and code status? My working problem is [problem]. The immediate plan is [plan]. If [trigger], we will [escalation step]. Orders are owned by [name], and disposition is [plan]. What are we missing?”


Use this when nursing or outreach is already actively managing the patient. The goal is not to slow the response; it is to prevent parallel, conflicting plans.

No shock for asystole.

Learning Points

Sustained polymorphic VT is unstable: shock immediately with unsynchronized high-energy defibrillation because synchronization may fail. If recurrent TdP with long QT, give magnesium, address bradycardia/QT drivers, and ask for expert help for overdrive pacing or isoproterenol.
QT prolongation more dangerous with slow HR

The bedside nurse can help prepare pacing before the patient loses pulses.
Ask:

“Are pads on? Who can help with sedation? Who is calling cardiology/ICU?”

Do not wait until arrest to organize the room.

title: Case 5
text:
EKG Analysis

Options: transcutaneous pacing (+sedation), transvenous pacing (requires line, expertise)

title: Case 5
text:
Teaching Points:

Complete heart block = AV dissociation.
Atropine is reasonable in unstable bradycardia, but do not wait on it when high-grade or infranodal block is likely. Prepare pacing/pressors and transvenous pacing early.
Always have pacing pads in place during rapid responses.

Transcutaneous pacing will require sedation

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Escalation, disposition, and closure
Learners will practice:

Deciding when the current room is no longer safe
Calling the right resource early
Naming disposition, orders, ownership, and triggers
Ending a code with team check, family plan, and debrief

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
The core question
Is this patient safe here with current people, monitoring, and resources?
Ask:

What is the risk in the next 5 minutes?
What resource is missing now?
Where does this patient need to be?
Who owns the patient until they get there?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
VA RRT case
Elderly man, immediately hypoxemic after transfusion.
RR 24. SpO2 82% on 2 L.
Now worsening: tripoding, accessory muscle use, 100% FiO2 face mask, SpO2 upper 80s.

Prompt: What do you say out loud now?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Escalate before the room fails



Signal
Action




Oxygenation or airway failure
Code/anesthesia


ICU monitoring or drips
ICU


STEMI/cath physiology
Cath


Focal neuro deficit
Stroke


Shock, PE, VT storm, device question
Shock/PERT/TICU by site



If this may become a code: bed out/down, pads on, airway/CPR access clear.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Every rapid needs an endpoint
A rapid response should end with one of these:

code blue
ICU transfer
rarely, a procedure
stabilized on the floor
goals-of-care transition

Always hand off to the team assuming care.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Disposition huddle
Try:

“Disposition is [ICU / floor / code / goals-of-care].”


“Follow-up is owned by [me / primary team].”


“The person for the nurse to call is [name/team].”


“Are there concerns we have not addressed?”

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
How long to continue?
Around 30 minutes, make an explicit stop/continue huddle. This is an anchor, not a stopping rule.
Modify earlier or later based on rhythm trajectory, witnessed/monitored status, reversible causes, ROSC signs, bridge options, goals, and team input.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Modify the anchor


Longer

witnessed/monitored
shockable or improving
reversible cause in progress
possible ROSC
bridge option


Shorter

unwitnessed/unmonitored
asystole/PEA without change
no reversible target
no ROSC signs
no bridge option

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text: Duration informs prognosis

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
What duration does not decide
Duration matters. It informs the huddle; it does not decide alone.
ETCO2 alone should not decide stopping or continuing.
Out-of-hospital TOR rules do not automatically decide in-hospital codes.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
How to stop ACLS

Summarize


“[duration] CPR, persistent [rhythm], no ROSC, and no remaining reversible intervention likely to change the outcome.”


Ask


“Does anyone see something we have not tried?”


Announce


“One final rhythm and pulse check. If unchanged, we will stop CPR.”

After stopping:

Declare time of death.
Assign family update.
Thank the team.
Plan a brief debrief.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
After the event: assign tasks

Family update: [name]
Documentation/time: recorder
Attending/workflow: primary team
Debrief: [time/place]

What went well? What changes? Does anyone need support?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Summary

Unsafe here? Call early.
Moving where? Name disposition.
Who follows up? Name owner and callback.
Ending how? Team check, family plan, debrief.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Working with nurse-led response teams
Align decisions, expertise, and plan in the first 60 seconds
Learners will practice:

Naming key decisions
Finding who has patient-specific expertise
Making the decision logic public
Closing the loop

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Nurse/outreach teams are a resource
Bedside and outreach nurses are often already working the problem.
They may know:

what changed and how fast
what has been tried or failed
what resources are missing
whether the patient feels unsafe for the unit

The resident adds synthesis, orders, escalation, and disposition.
Goal: one shared plan.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Case start
You are called because a bedside nurse asked the critical care outreach nurse to assess a patient.
Formal RRT has not yet been called.
The patient is newly confused, tachypneic, and on escalating oxygen.
The outreach nurse is at bedside. The primary intern is present but quiet. The charge nurse is looking for the primary team.
Prompt: What decisions do you need to make, and who can help?

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 1: Name the key decisions
Try:

“I’m [name], the senior medicine resident responding. Let’s name the decisions we need to make right now.”

Ask:

What problem are we treating first?
Is the patient safe here?
What information would change our plan?
What resource or destination decision is coming next?

Decision ownership still matters. First, improve decision quality by getting the right expertise into the plan.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 2: Find the expertise
Ask for the knowledge you need:

“Bedside nurse: what changed from baseline?”


“Outreach nurse: what have you tried, and what worries you most?”


“Primary team: baseline, code status, active plan?”


“Charge nurse: what resource is missing?”

Then listen before committing to a plan.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
section: Move 3: Make the shared plan public
text:
Move 3: Make the shared plan public
Use the same structure:

“I think [problem] is the issue. I’m worried about [risk]. My plan is [plan].”

Then ask:

“What are we missing?”

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 4: Make concern actionable

“What feels unsafe?”


“What trigger should move us now?”

Name a trigger. Escalate together.
Concern is a risk signal.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 5: Close before leaving
Check with the team, then name:

disposition
order owner
patient owner
trigger


“Before I leave, what concerns are we missing?”

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Common failure modes

Ignore work already done
Ask for chart review, not trajectory
Give a plan without an owner
Leave without destination or trigger
Treat concern as anxiety
Miss team expertise

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Summary

Name the key decisions.
Find the patient-specific expertise.
Make the shared plan public.
Close the loop on disposition, owner, and trigger.
